title: Load Balancers Explained
intro: Once you have more than one server, something has to decide which server handles each request. That's the load balancer.

slides.heading: What it does
slides.subtitle: A traffic manager for your servers.
slides.explain: The load balancer sits between users and your servers. Users connect to one address, and it forwards each request to a healthy server behind it.
points: One public address for many servers

slides.heading: Algorithms
slides.subtitle: How it picks a server.
slides.explain: Different strategies suit different workloads. Round robin is the simplest; least connections copes better when some requests take much longer.
points: Least connections: pick the least busy
IP hash: same client, same server

slides.heading: Health checks
slides.subtitle: Avoiding broken servers.
slides.explain: The load balancer regularly checks each server. If one stops responding, it's taken out of rotation until it recovers, so users don't hit it.

slides.heading: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
slides.subtitle: How deep it looks.
slides.explain: A Layer 4 balancer routes by IP and port only, so it's very fast. A Layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request and can route by URL path or headers.
points: L7: smart routing, e.g. /api to API servers

slides.heading: Don't add a weak spot
slides.subtitle: The balancer can fail too.
slides.explain: If the load balancer goes down, everything behind it does too. Production setups run at least two, or use a managed cloud load balancer.
points: Managed options handle this for you

scenario.situation: A site runs three servers behind a round-robin load balancer, and one server's disk fills up.
scenario.problem: Without health checks, one in three requests still goes to the broken server, so a third of users see errors.
scenario.fix: Turn on health checks. The balancer notices the failing server within seconds and sends traffic only to the two healthy ones.
scenario.takeaway: A load balancer without health checks spreads failures too.
